intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive distal hereditary motor neuronopathy-9 (HMNR9) is caused by homozygous mutation in the COQ7 gene (601683) on chromosome 16p12.3.

paragraphs.text: Autosomal recessive distal hereditary motor neuronopathy-9 (HMNR9) is a progressive, length-dependent motor neuropathy. Distal weakness and atrophy begin in the lower limbs in late childhood or early adolescence and later involve the hands. Pes cavus is common, sensation is preserved, and some patients have pyramidal signs (Jacquier et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2023). The disorder results from loss of COQ7 function and is associated with reduced coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) and accumulation of the COQ7 substrate 6-demethoxycoenzyme Q10 (Jacquier et al., 2023; Smith et al., 2023).

paragraphs.text: Jacquier et al. (2023) reported 3 Portuguese sibs with distal hereditary motor neuropathy (dHMN): 2 brothers aged 36 and 42 years and a sister aged 25 years. Their parents were healthy and not consanguineous. Early development was normal, and walking difficulties began between ages 9 and 12 years. Distal weakness started in the lower limbs, mainly as loss of foot dorsiflexion, and progressed to involve the hands between ages 13 and 32 years. All 3 sibs had pes cavus and amyotrophy or distal deficit in the lower limbs and hands. Their sensory examination and cranial nerves were normal, and none had a cognitive disorder. Two sibs had pyramidal signs: one had brisk reflexes with a Hoffman sign, and the other had a left Babinski sign. The authors suggested that dHMN with pyramidal features indicated upper motor neuron involvement. The 42-year-old eldest brother developed foot drop at age 10 years and needed ankle-foot orthoses from about age 20. He had hand weakness from age 22. At age 42, he had complete loss of foot plantar flexion and dorsiflexion, with distal amyotrophy. The 25-year-old sister reported reduced perception of cold and warm on her feet, but her sensory examination was normal. All 3 sibs remained ambulant. In 2 of the sibs, electroneuromyography showed a pure motor axonal neuropathy that mainly affected the distal lower limbs, and needle examination showed fibrillations and reduced motor unit recruitment. The index patient had normal brain and spinal cord MRI, echocardiography, ECG and audiometry. Creatine kinase was mildly elevated at 215 U/l.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2023) reported 3 sibs born to Syrian first-cousin parents: a 24-year-old woman, a 23-year-old man and a 12-year-old boy. They had a progressive length-dependent motor neuropathy. Distal weakness began at 10 to 14 years of age, and distal muscle atrophy affected the lower limbs more than the upper limbs. Sensation in all modalities and deep tendon reflexes were preserved. Electrodiagnostic testing showed reduced distal motor amplitudes with preserved sensory responses. Needle EMG showed distal chronic reinnervation without active denervation. Gene panels for Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, spinal muscular atrophy, distal hereditary motor neuropathy and mtDNA were negative. Whole-body muscle MRI was performed in 2 of the sibs. It showed normal proximal musculature and significant distal muscle wasting. Moderate to severe fat infiltration began at the distal third of the thigh and was most pronounced in both calves, especially the soleus and gastrocnemius. A vastus lateralis biopsy from 1 sib showed neurogenic atrophy, with angular atrophic fibers (sometimes in groups), pyknotic nuclear clumps, group atrophy and fiber type grouping. There were no ragged red fibers and no cytochrome oxidase-negative fibers.

paragraphs.text: Wongkittichote et al. (2023) identified 5 new patients with COQ7-related primary CoQ10 deficiency, adding to 9 previously reported patients from 7 families. They described 2 clinical presentations. The first had neonatal onset, with severe neuromuscular, cardiorespiratory and renal involvement. The second had late onset, with progressive neuropathy, lower-extremity weakness, abnormal gait and variable developmental delay.

paragraphs.text: In the Syrian family reported by Smith et al. (2023), congenital deafness did not segregate with the motor neuropathy. The deafness was explained by a homozygous c.35delG (p.Gly12ValfsTer2) variant in the GJB2 gene, for which both parents were heterozygous carriers.

paragraphs.text: Jacquier et al. (2023) used HPLC-MS/MS to study fibroblasts from the index patient of their Portuguese family. CoQ10 was markedly reduced (12.5 pmol/mg protein, compared with 71.5 pmol/mg in controls), and the fibroblasts contained the COQ7 substrate 6-demethoxycoenzyme Q10 (6-DMQ). 6-DMQ was also detected in the patient's plasma. After 14 days of supplementation with the bypass precursor 2,4-dihydroxybenzoic acid, CoQ10 rose slightly (to 18.8 pmol/mg) and 6-DMQ normalized, which confirmed a loss of COQ7 activity.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2023) found that cultured fibroblasts from the 3 affected Syrian sibs had on average 87% less CoQ10 than fibroblasts from the carrier father and an unaffected sib. The affected fibroblasts also accumulated the COQ7 substrate DMQ10, which was undetectable in carriers. COQ7 protein in affected fibroblasts was 85% lower than in carriers, while PDSS2 levels were unchanged. In muscle from 1 affected sib, COQ7 protein was undetectable and CoQ10 was 67% lower than in a control (63 vs 192.7 ng/mg protein), but no DMQ10 was detected. In permeabilized muscle from this sib, FCCP-induced maximal respiration and complex IV activity were reduced, H2O2 emission was increased, and there were fewer supercomplexes containing complexes I and IV. Fibroblasts from the affected sibs had preserved basal respiration but reduced maximal and spare respiratory capacity. They also had higher basal extracellular acidification, a bioenergetic profile favoring glycolysis, and impaired switching between ATP production pathways. Complex I activity, citrate synthase activity and viability in galactose medium were normal.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of HMNR9 is autosomal recessive. In the families reported by Jacquier et al. (2023) and Smith et al. (2023), affected sibs were homozygous for COQ7 mutations and their unaffected parents were heterozygous. Wongkittichote et al. (2023) noted that biallelic pathogenic COQ7 variants cause primary CoQ10 deficiency, consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

paragraphs.text: Jacquier et al. (2023) performed whole-exome sequencing in both parents and all 3 affected sibs of a Portuguese family with HMNR9. They identified a homozygous c.3G-T variant (p.Met1?) in the COQ7 gene, which changes the canonical ATG start codon of isoform 1 (NM_016138.5) to ATT. All 3 patients were homozygous and the unaffected parents were heterozygous, and Sanger sequencing confirmed these genotypes. The variant was absent from ExAC and was found once in the heterozygous state in gnomAD (allele frequency 0.000004065). The alternative start codons used by isoforms 2 and 3 were predicted to be unaffected. In fibroblasts from the index patient, COQ7 mRNA was decreased only modestly (by 21% and 17% with 2 primer pairs), but COQ7 protein was barely detectable. Mitochondrial content was similar to controls. In SH-EP neuroblastoma cells transfected with FLAG-tagged constructs, the mutant protein localized like wildtype but was reduced by 85%, with unchanged mRNA levels. The authors interpreted this as a translational defect.
